text:
AUDIO XX SYSTEM ASSESSMENT

17 September 2026

EVERSOLO DMP-A6 · CHORD HUGO · JOB INTEGRATED · WLM DIVA MONITOR

System review
The assessment

This system is organised around a high-sensitivity loudspeaker. A loudspeaker reported at 95dB sensitivity asks very little of amplification whose circuit the maker ties to the JOB 225, a 125W design, so on every figure available, amplifier power is very unlikely to be this system’s constraint. That is a supported reading rather than an established one: the sensitivity figure is the maker’s claim as a publication reported it, not a published specification; the amplifier’s own rating is unpublished — the JOB 225 figure is the maker’s stated reference point, not a rating for this unit. How this combination voices is a separate question, taken up below.

How this system fits together

The shape of this system is not yet settled. The Eversolo DMP-A6, the Chord Hugo and the JOB INTegrated’s onboard conversion can each perform digital-to-analogue conversion, and which one actually sits in the signal path decides where the system’s character originates — a different answer makes this a materially different system. That is a fact about connections, not about quality, and only you can settle it.

The first relationship I would examine here is the JOB INTegrated driving the WLM Diva Monitor — but the evidence held is not enough to say whether it is actually limiting anything. That turns on the JOB INTegrated’s rated output, the WLM Diva Monitor’s sensitivity and its nominal impedance, none of which is established. Until those figures are on the record, whether the amplifier limits this system stays an open question — the one that most limits this assessment.

What I would do

One thing this component list does not tell me is where digital-to-analogue conversion actually happens: the Eversolo DMP-A6, the Chord Hugo and the JOB INTegrated’s onboard conversion are all capable of performing it, and which one sits in the signal path depends on how they are connected — something I will not guess from a component list. Any advice about the conversion stage would change with that answer, so before offering it: how are you connecting them?

What remains unknown

I don’t have reliable exact-product listening evidence for the Eversolo DMP-A6, the Chord Hugo and the WLM Diva monitor, so I won’t pretend to know how this particular combination sounds. A published review of these exact units would establish what specifications cannot.

question: What if I swapped the WLMs for Boenicke W5s?
text:
If you mean the Boenicke W5, I’d treat that as a change of system direction, not an automatic upgrade. Your Diva Monitors’ reported high sensitivity gives the JOB an easy job in terms of power demand. From my general knowledge of the compact W5 design, I’d expect less sensitivity and greater dependence on placement—but the exact version matters, and I can’t establish its load or output limits here.

The JOB is a reasonable amplifier to audition them with: listening results for the related JOB 225 suggest capable control, though that doesn’t guarantee headroom with the Boenickes at your listening distance. I’d pay particular attention to bass weight and whether musical peaks remain effortless at your normal volume. Small speakers can create a spacious presentation without necessarily matching a larger speaker’s scale; I wouldn’t promise either outcome for this swap.

Keep the Eversolo → Hugo → JOB chain unchanged for a home comparison. That lets you judge the speaker–room change without also changing DACs. Which W5 version are you considering, how large is your room, and what would you like to improve over the Divas? Those answers would determine whether this is a promising move or simply a different set of compromises.

question: Would you actually do that, in my place?
text:
No—not as a blind swap. In your place, I’d keep the WLMs unless a home audition gave me a clear reason to change.

Your Diva Monitors’ reported high sensitivity, together with the JOB’s maker-stated power-circuit relationship to the JOB 225, suggests useful headroom. That doesn’t prove perfect synergy, but you haven’t identified a shortcoming that the Boenickes would solve. I also don’t know which W5 version you mean or whether it would preserve the scale and ease you want at your listening level.

I’d leave the Eversolo → Hugo → JOB chain intact and borrow the Boenickes if they interest you. Buy only if they make music consistently more convincing in your room—not merely different. For now, keeping the Divas is my recommendation.

question: What I really love here is the intimacy and connection — I don't want to lose that.
text:
Then I’d be more reluctant to replace the Divas. You’ve identified something this particular system already delivers for you: intimacy and emotional connection. That matters more than a possible upgrade in individual hi-fi attributes.

The WLMs’ coaxial layout could contribute to that sense of a unified presentation, but I can’t separate its contribution from your room, placement and the Hugo–JOB chain. Nor do I know whether the particular Boenicke W5 version you’re considering would preserve it. A larger or more striking soundstage wouldn’t necessarily mean greater intimacy.

I’d keep your system as it stands unless a home audition proved otherwise. With the same electronics and closely matched listening levels, play familiar voices and small ensembles: does the performer still feel present, and do you stay absorbed in the music? If the Boenickes impress you but weaken that connection, they’re not an upgrade for you.

question: Say I had about $5k for one change — where would you put it?
text:
I’d keep the $5k for now rather than replace a component. You’ve told me what this system gets right—intimacy and connection—but not what it fails to deliver. There isn’t yet a clear target worth risking that balance for.

If you want to pursue one improvement, I’d put room and speaker setup first, starting with an in-room assessment—not a $5k treatment package. Placement, listening distance and reflections can affect vocal focus and the balance between direct sound and room sound. That makes them relevant to your priority, although I don’t know whether your room actually needs intervention. More absorption isn’t automatically better.

I’d leave the Eversolo, Hugo, JOB and Divas together while exploring that. What, if anything, interrupts the connection now—boomy bass, an edge on voices, congestion when music gets busy, or nothing? That answer would give the money a purpose; without it, my recommendation is to change nothing.

question: Give me specific components with model numbers, and why those in my system.
text:
I’d shortlist these three—but for different needs, not as guaranteed upgrades. These are audition suggestions from my general knowledge; I haven’t established how they’ll sound in your room. For the amplifiers, I’d look used and confirm current pricing against your $5k limit.

Luxman L-505uXII integrated amplifier — the conventional amplifier alternative. It would replace the JOB, leaving the Eversolo, Hugo and Divas in place. That preserves the speakers already giving you the connection you value while testing whether different amplification improves vocal substance and low-level involvement. Those are listening questions, not qualities I can promise the Luxman will deliver over your JOB. I wouldn’t buy it without that comparison.
Leben CS300XS integrated amplifier — the more exploratory choice. This is a tube-amplifier route worth considering with the Divas’ reported high sensitivity. At a design-class level, tube amplification can change tonal balance and bass damping through its interaction with speaker impedance; that can be attractive or counterproductive. I don’t know the Divas’ impedance curve, so sensitivity alone doesn’t establish compatibility. Audition for intimacy and bass control, noise and headroom—not simply “tube warmth.”
REL T/9x subwoofer — only if missing bass foundation is the problem. This would retain your entire existing chain and add low-frequency support. A carefully integrated sub can supply foundation without asking you to abandon the speakers you love, but room modes and excessive level can also obscure their intimacy. Check the connection arrangement with your JOB before purchase; positioning and adjustment would be central to the result.

My first amplifier audition would be the Luxman; my actual spending recommendation remains conditional. If you want fuller low-frequency weight, investigate the REL instead. If nothing is missing and connection is already exceptional, I wouldn’t spend $5k merely to replace the JOB—or the WLMs.

text:
Yes—in your place, I’d leave it alone. Your Eversolo → Hugo → JOB → WLM Diva system already gives you the intimacy and connection you value most, and you haven’t named a persistent weakness. That’s a good reason to keep it, not a failure to pursue something better.

My earlier component shortlist was more speculative than your situation warranted. Those are possible auditions, not demonstrated improvements over what you own. A different amplifier or speaker could shift the balance without making the music more involving.

Keep the $5k. If a specific frustration emerges during ordinary listening, address that—not the existence of an upgrade budget. For now, enjoy the combination you’ve found.

question: Everyone tells me to just replace the oldest thing. Is that right here?
text:
No. Replace the part causing a problem, not the part with the earliest birthday. Age is a reason to check condition—not a reliable ranking of sound quality.

In your system, the Dynaco A35s deserve inspection, not automatic retirement. If both speakers work consistently and suit your room and listening levels, keeping them is reasonable. If they’re faulty, repair may make sense; if they’re healthy but don’t deliver the bass, clarity or volume you want, replacement becomes a meaningful option. Those are different decisions.

The NAD also warrants a condition and setup check: channel imbalance, crackling, hum or distortion would justify attention, though each needs tracing rather than automatically blaming the receiver. I don’t know its present condition or how much clean output it delivers into your Dynacos. The newer Topping isn’t automatically superior in importance, but there’s no clear reason here to replace it.

My earlier ranking was where to investigate first, not a shopping order. Before spending, check placement, confirm both speakers sound alike with a mono recording, and identify what you actually want improved. A healthy old component that meets your needs isn’t a bottleneck merely because newer alternatives exist.

question: What if I put a Rega Elex Mk4 in place of the NAD?
text:
The Rega Elex Mk4 is a plausible replacement, but I wouldn’t call it a proven upgrade in your system. It would make sense if you want a dedicated stereo amplifier, no longer need the NAD’s AV functions, or have identified a problem with the NAD. “Stereo integrated” alone doesn’t guarantee better sound than “AV receiver.”

With the Topping retained as DAC and the A35s retained as speakers, an amplifier change could help if the NAD is introducing noise, channel imbalance, unwanted processing or running out of clean output. It won’t fix room-induced bass unevenness or ageing speaker components. I don’t have enough information about the two amplifiers’ performance into your Dynacos to promise more control, clearer detail or better dynamics—and I wouldn’t substitute a supposed “Rega sound” for that missing comparison.

My recommendation: audition, rather than buy on reputation. Keep the Topping, speaker positions and recordings unchanged; match listening loudness closely and compare at both normal and demanding levels. Listen for a more stable central voice, cleaner busy passages and less strain—not simply a louder or brighter presentation. Check that the Rega accommodates every source and function you actually use.

If the improvement is clear and repeatable, the swap is justified. If it’s subtle or uncertain, keep the NAD and investigate the speakers and room first.

question: I listen in a small room at modest volume, mostly evenings.
text:
That makes the case for replacing the NAD weaker. In a small room at modest volume, maximum amplifier output is less likely to be your main constraint. Unless the NAD has a fault or an unsuitable processing mode engaged, I wouldn’t expect an amplifier swap to be the first thing to pursue.

For evening listening, I’d prioritise even bass at your seat, a stable stereo image, and volume adjustment that keeps both channels balanced at low levels. Speaker placement and listening position can matter substantially here. Also, our hearing becomes less sensitive to bass as volume falls: if the system sounds a little lightweight late at night, that doesn’t necessarily mean the NAD lacks power. Suitable tonal adjustment, if available, may help more than changing amplifiers.

Keep the Topping and don’t retire the Dynacos on age alone. Consider the Rega only after an audition at your actual evening volume—not a louder showroom demonstration. I don’t know whether it would improve low-level control or audible noise over your particular NAD. If the present system is quiet, balanced and satisfying at those levels, changing nothing is a sound recommendation.

question: Given that, would modernizing actually get me anything I would hear?
text:
Yes, potentially—but replacing old equipment with newer equipment isn’t itself an audible upgrade. In your small room at modest evening levels, you’re more likely to hear changes in speaker balance, placement and low-volume behaviour than benefits from greater amplifier power.

The Rega-for-NAD swap is an uncertain return. If your NAD is quiet, keeps voices centred at low volume and plays cleanly, the difference could be small. I can’t promise the Elex Mk4 would bring more detail or body with your Dynacos. Audition it at your usual evening level before spending; even a small loudness difference can make the comparison misleading.

Different speakers—or useful room/EQ adjustment—offer more scope for an obvious change, though not automatically an improvement. Healthy A35s may already give you a balance you prefer. If bass is boomy or certain notes disappear, investigate placement first. If everything becomes thin only when you turn it down, suitable loudness compensation or gentle tonal adjustment may help more directly than a new amplifier.

My recommendation is to keep the Topping and postpone the Rega purchase. First identify one repeatable shortcoming at your normal listening level. If you can’t name one, modernization is more likely to buy features, convenience or peace of mind than a meaningful sonic improvement.

question: Would you, though? In my position?
text:
No—I would keep the E-600 in your position, based on what you’ve told me. You haven’t identified a listening problem that replacing it would solve. With your DP-450 and SHL5 Plus, there is no demonstrated amplifier shortfall, and I don’t know enough about the L-509Z’s behaviour in this pairing to promise a sonic improvement.

I would reconsider if you regularly want louder, cleaner peaks than the Accuphase can deliver—or if a level-matched home audition makes you consistently prefer the Luxman at your normal listening volume. Either is a valid reason to change; the idea that the Harbeths necessarily need “more than 30 watts” isn’t.

For now, I’d keep the system and the money.

question: I sit close, about eight feet, and I never listen loud. I care about tone and texture above everything.
text:
That makes me more confident: I would keep the E-600. At eight feet, with no loud listening, amplifier headroom is less likely to be your practical constraint. The Harbeths’ modest sensitivity still matters, but it doesn’t make the Accuphase’s 30-watt rating an automatic mismatch.

For your priorities—tone and texture—more power isn’t itself an improvement. Nor does Class A automatically guarantee those qualities. I can’t promise that the L-509Z would render voices or instruments more convincingly in your system; that would need listening, not an inference from amplifier topology or price.

I’d leave the DP-450, E-600 and SHL5 Plus together. Only pursue the Luxman if a level-matched home audition at your normal quiet volume gives you a consistent preference for instrumental timbre and the way notes develop and decay. You don’t currently have a demonstrated problem that needs buying your way out of.

question: With that in mind, what — if anything — would you change first?
text:
I’d change no component first. I’d start with placement—and only if there’s something about the sound you want to improve. At eight feet and quiet levels, there’s no clear reason to make amplifier headroom your first target, and no established reason to single out the DP-450.

For tone and texture, try small, reversible changes to the Harbeths’ distance from the wall behind them and their toe-in. Boundary reinforcement and room reflections can alter instrumental body and obscure subtle decays. Keep your seat and volume fixed, change one thing at a time, and mark the original positions. Listen for voices retaining both body and intelligibility—not simply for a leaner sound that initially seems more detailed.

One other consideration: at low volume, our hearing becomes less sensitive to bass, which can make otherwise natural reproduction feel thinner. If that is what you hear, a modest tonal adjustment—if available in your setup—is a more direct experiment than replacing the amplifier.

If you already find the tone convincing and textures easy to follow, I’d stop there. What I’d want to identify before spending anything is a specific shortcoming: too little body, excessive warmth, hard vocal edges, or textures that blur together. Each points toward a different remedy.

question: And if the answer is nothing, say so plainly.
text:
Nothing. I would keep your DP-450, E-600 and Harbeth SHL5 Plus as they are.

At eight feet, without loud listening, you haven’t described a limitation that calls for more amplifier power. And there’s no clear basis to expect the Luxman to improve the tone and texture you value.

Unless something specific is bothering you, I wouldn’t turn placement or room treatment into a project either. Enjoy the system; you don’t need to find a fault to justify keeping it.
